utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution this morning. For the next witness we'll be joined by Belinda Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Stanisic Defence today appearing, myself, Zecevic, and Mr. Slobodan Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, for the Zupljanin Defence today, Dragan Krgovic, Brent Hicks, and Eric Tully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you. Before the witness takes the stand again is there any --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Before the witness takes the stand again, is there anything that we need address?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think we are all aware of the -- the change of order of witnesses from the e-mail correspondence yesterday with the senior legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please have the witness back into court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The only thing I'm asking, Your Honours, is I'm afraid that -- maybe the court clerk can assist. We are having problems getting to e-court at the moment, and I can't remember which document I'd got to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 717.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 717, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, sir, I would remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm told that I haven't exhibited yesterday's -- I have exhibited it. Thank you. And could I have up, please, very briefly 65 ter 719.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, this is simply to note, isn't it, that on the 7th of July, effectively in accordance with instructions that came, I think, from the Main Board or from the government, the Crisis Staff - we can see it; this is set out in item 3 - was renamed the War Presidency, but effectively the members remained the same.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty whether every person remained on the Presidency. I also cannot explain why the term was changed from Crisis Staff to War Presidency, because shortly afterwards, the executive organs became functional again, including the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, don't worry why, but this is purely so that the Trial Chamber -- we are going to hear some more evidence about it to understand what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P87, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Could we have up, please, 65 ter number 720.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again another extract from the minutes, this time, as we see, called the War Presidency, following day. And it says in item 1, the work of the SJB -- due to problems in the work of the SJB, a decision has been made to use the hall in the Pilana, the sawmill temporarily as a prison, and he recommended that all detained persons be transferred there. Can we take it from that that there were so many prisoners that the prison that you pointed out in Kotor Varos and the police station couldn't hold them?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Bad question by me. No what? Is that right, that there were too many prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you are just on the edge of putting leading questions to this witness. And he is still just a normal viva voce witness, so I guess we should ask the witness what he makes out of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already explained the issue of Pilana, there is no proof that any detainees spent prolonged periods of time in Pilana, those who were accommodated there spent only a short time there and were mainly brought in for security reasons. As for any grammatical or stylistic errors of the minutes, this is something I cannot comment upon. But I know for certain that Pilana was not a prison in which detainees were held for long periods of time. It was rather used a as point from which they were sent onwards or to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. That wasn't my question. That's why leading questions are sometimes helpful. What was the reason, however, that there had to be a temporary prison?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that yesterday. The reason was that people in the field were left unprotected, and frequently they came in themselves seeking protection. One of the main reasons why people were put in Pilana was precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it's these people, and they included women and children, is that right, were being put into the sawmill for their own protection?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what, to your knowledge, sir, happened to the women in the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As all other detainees they only spent a few days in Pilana until there was a suitable transport or convoy for them to go to the other side or to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did anything, to your knowledge, sir, happen to the women who were in the sawmill, for however short a period of time?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I knew of no incidents. Much, much later, I heard that there were one or two rapings. I don't know what the exact figure was, but I'm certain that it did not occur in great numbers and that it did not happen to all the women.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why are you certain it didn't happen in great numbers?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm absolutely certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I'm asking you why you have such certainty?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it didn't happen that way, and it was not a mass occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How do you know that, sir? Were you there at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never went to Pilana. I told you already that I know that people did not spend long periods of time there, that they left rather quickly, and I know from the people who were in charge that such things did not happen on mass. I cannot confirm for the one or two cases of rape, I don't even know who did that, but what I heard was that there were one or two incidents of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this position I cannot tell you with certainty who I heard it from. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was this report -- well, Savo Tepic was in charge of the police, wasn't he? Did he tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that Savo Tepic was in charge of the police, but I don't know whether he told me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness -- sorry, Mr. Djekanovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think I heard you say that the people who were kept at Pilana, for the largest part of them, they came at their own free will to seek protection; is that correct? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, one could say so. They didn't arrive in Pilana. They came before the municipal building in town seeking protection. Some of them were even brought in, in an organised fashion to protect them. Some of them were accommodated in the hotel, but then there were too many of them and the hotel was shelled, hence Pilana was mostly used for the accommodation of precisely those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then why is it that the minutes of this exhibit show that Pilana was used temporarily as a prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of terminology, I don't know why someone used the word "prison." Several facilities were used to that end for a few evenings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sir, you signed the minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Although there is no signature of mine, but yes, there you go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So they were words that you had either chosen or accepted, namely to classify the Pilana sawmill as a prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that it says that it was a prison. I do not dispute that. But I don't know to what end it was used. If there is additional proof that people spent prolonged period of time there and were detained there, then I will accept that, but I can tell you that they were not kept for long periods of time there and that they were mainly brought in for the reasons I specified. It is possible that there were detainees per se, but again, even they stayed shortly. And in particular, children and women were never detained. They were never detainees; they were never kept in custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And did you know whether any separation was made between those who were detained and those who came at their own free will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One final question on this aspect. When you heard, whoever you heard from, that women had been raped, did you raise the matter with either Savo Tepic or in any meetings that you had with Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With full responsibility I claim that concerning this incident, the one or two incidents, I heard only half a year or full year later. I was not aware of it as it was taking place. It could be that I only heard of it a full year later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And there in the second part of item 1 Dubocanin tells you that a decision has been made for the special unit to withdraw from Kotor Varos; is that right? Tells the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he tell you who had made that decision?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not, and we did not insist upon knowing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P88 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next could we have up 65 ter number 723.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the sake of full truth, I wanted to say that the special unit that most questions referred to was never used to guard or secure Pilana. I wish to make that known. The members of the Special Police unit did not guard or secure Pilana. They did not guard other secure any other facilities, save for those where they were billeted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that in the course of the proofing as well. I told you they were not trained for that, and they did not wish to stand guard or secure facilities. It was not their intention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you didn't tell me anything in proofing because I didn't proof you. But, sorry, it doesn't matter who you told or what, but what -- why -- sorry, start this one again. How do you know that they were not trained for that, did not wish to stand guard?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed that topic on several occasions, and I know that along -- even along the axis or lines of attack which they pursued, they refused to stand guard once they had taken up any territory, so they would go into combat and come back. They always disliked securing or standing guard anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a matter of interest, Mr. Djekanovic, have you spoken to anybody overnight about this evidence?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one. Yesterday, for example, I took a walk to the beach and saw no one, spoke to no one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That will do. We looked yesterday at a number of documents where there were complaints about what the Special Police were doing to the prisoners at the SJB. Do you remember all those documents? The minutes of your meetings?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the documents we went through yesterday is something that I use to jog my memory, but I don't leaf through them every day. Once I came here and as I was getting ready for the testimony, I did go through some of them, and of course those I saw yesterday served as a reminder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look, I really don't want to rehearse all of yesterday's evidence, but you agreed what was being raised at the Crisis Staff meeting was the complaints about the behaviour of the Special Police which included beating up prisoners who were being held in the SJB and elsewhere. Now, are you now saying that is not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it's better for Ms. Korner to show the exact document to the witness. What she is now quoting to the witness is not something you can find in any documents. The witness did not speak to this part. Perhaps she should provide a transcript reference or the document she has in mind, otherwise I contest that such things were not said in this way before this Tribunal yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is my recollection. I do not have the time now because I'm anxious to finish with this witness in chief, but I will, however, find the part of the transcript yesterday when I finish my examination-in-chief. But I'm sure it's a matter for the recollection of the Trial Chamber whatever Defence counsel may say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, are you saying now, Mr. Djekanovic, let's very clearly understand you, that as far as you are concerned, the Special Police never stood as guards over people who had been captured or brought into the prisons and the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that in full responsibility, and I repeat for umpteenth time, the special unit did not stand guard or secure those facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whether they were officially on guard or securing the facilities, to your knowledge, did they go to those places of imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who went where individually, that is something I truly don't know. They did go to the police station, I know that much. In the health centre, they had their accommodation. As for their visits to the sawmill, I don't know about that. I don't know whether there's any proof. I know, though, that in the sawmill, save for the few incidents you mentioned, there are no other incidents. There were a few beatings in the police station, but you were trying to proof that this was a daily occurrence which lasted for months on end. At the beginning of certain combat operations this things may have happened in the course of the first few couple of days, but it didn't cover entire days and people coming in and leaving as they wished. There were certain incidents at the police station, but I wash my hands of that because there was nothing I could do at the time. And I'm quite certain that they did not happen on such a scale as you are trying to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, may I just remind you that you are not being interviewed here as a suspect. That you are not being charged or investigated in any way for your actions during the conflict. So by virtue of this, you are required to tell the truth, and I should remind you that there is a severe penalty for providing false testimony to this court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand you fully, but I don't know whether you know that I was interrogated as a suspect and that all of my statements and interviews were given in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We are fully aware of your having been once interviewed as a suspect, but that is now behind us, and you are no more a suspect in front of these proceedings. You are a witness, and you are obliged to tell the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move, please, to the 14th of July, which I hope is now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Under item 1, we see that the War Presidency was concluding: "...it was not satisfied with the results achieved so far and the current military and security situation." Was further concluded, "...that General Talic and Stojan Zupljanin have to be contacted urgently in order to inform them of our dissatisfaction with developments so far and task them with creating conditions needed to accelerate the operation." Exactly what operation did you want accelerated by the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly cannot confirm what operation exactly this is referring to, and whether it is actually referring to an operation. But I can conclude that we were not satisfied at the time, and we were not satisfied because almost throughout the entire territory in Kotor Varos municipality there were conflicts, there were daily burials because there were times when we would bury 12 to 13 people per day. And of course we weren't happy with that situation, nor were the people happy with it. There was no security on roads either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But an operation you want them to carry out, what was it that you wanted the police and the military to do, and do more efficiently?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any instance where the War Presidency requested the military police to carry out an operation, especially not a military operation. The military had their staff, of course, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop, stop, stop, please. I'm not asking about the military police, the military and the police. You were talking about General Talic and Stojan Zupljanin. So what operation did you want the military, full stop, and the police, full stop, to carry out?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The global request that we addressed to the military and the police was to provide security and safety in Kotor Varos municipality, and because there was a line of separation at Vlasic, we wanted them to ensure that there was security on the entire -- in the entire area of the municipality. But we did not request any operation nor did we specifically ask for any operation or mention it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it did nothing to do with cleansing Kotor Varos of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, and I stand by that. This has nothing to do with cleansing of the non-Serb population. And I told you that very soon thereafter we engaged in the municipal organs members of the non-Serb population to work for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, as cleaners as I recall. All right. Item 2 under the second dot: "Activities relating to moving out the population failed to meet expectations. This task must be dealt with in a much more organised fashion; an agency has to be established to handle these matters." The word is "moving out," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were moving out and that was something that could not be avoided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Activities relating to moving out the population," doesn't that suggest that there was some form of the population being moved, not them moving themselves?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that no one ever ordered actively an action to move out the population. There was a desire and an activity people asked to leave. There were problems with it. There were problems with the transportation of those people, with their protection, and there were also problems with people already taking money away and making people -- or making people cede their property to them, make them sign papers ceding their property. And there were activities to that effect to help those people, so that as they were moving out their problems were as minimal as possible. And in that sense, we did -- those were the activities, and I claim with full responsibility that that is how we handled these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I've already asked you about what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P89, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we very quickly, please, just look at 65 ter number 6 -- 728.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, we've got the B/C/S on the screen now, so can you find the part in that please, Mr. Djekanovic, where it talks about the relationship between the army and the police, which is just -- it's by the second dash -- third dash. Fourth dash, actually.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we just blow this up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Fourth dash, which begins: "The relationship between the army and police..."

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why was the War Presidency concerned about where the involvement of the army stops and responsibility is taken over by the police?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question. At some periods and at one period of over a month and a half, we had a problem because there was no joint staff or Joint Command and no coordination, so that frequently there were overlappings of authorities and competence over those units, so in that overlapping, of course there were problems. I mentioned yesterday that we had people engaged through the Territorial Defence who were supposed to be in the light brigade, the Municipal Light Brigade under the command of General Galic [as interpreted], but that unit remained without any commander for a long time. And our intervention was in that sense, we called on General Talic to improve the coordination, to improve the staff so that it is clearly defined whose area of responsibility what is. And this is all that this relates to, I don't know of anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, you said General Galic to begin with; was that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, could that please be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P90, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next one is already -- it's not, sorry, can I -- it's 65 ter number 10108, which will have to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's only one item I want to ask you about and that's item 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page in the English, and it's on the same page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The current issues that were discussed under this item were the behaviour of certain individuals - members of special units, and a proposal to Brigade command made by active-duty officers..." We saw on the 8th of July, that Dubocanin told you that the special unit was being pulled out, but on the 19th of July, it was still there; is that right? Is that right, Mr. Djekanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan said that it would be pulled out and not that it was pulled out. It is correct that he said that it would be pulled out, and it is also correct that it still remained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And still causing you problems apparently?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit it itself was not causing problems; it was individuals, members of the units who were causing the problems, and this is something we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but those members of that unit had a commander, either Ljuban Ecim in Banja Luka or Slobodan Dubocanin in Kotor Varos itself?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you complain to Dubocanin that he had told you that they were being pulled out, and yet, here they still were, causing members of his unit under police control still causing problems?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did complain, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was his reaction when you complained?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say, and you can see this from what we saw before, it -- there was a promise that the unit would be pulled out. However, a part of that unit was later on re-assigned and the number of members of the unit decreased. Some -- a part of the unit was transferred to another area, but some members remained behind and how many exactly, I don't know, as well as when the unit was pulled out completely from the town. But whenever there were problems we reacted and asked for this to be stopped, to be prevented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but as we will see, it still was going on. So did you approach again Stojan Zupljanin on whom -- with whom you were on friendly terms?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know on what basis you concluded that we were on friendly terms. We were only on official terms, and I addressed via the CSB or, rather, the station of public security and all communications with Zupljanin were through the station in Kotor Varos. The private encounters that we had a few days before does not imply that we had constant private communications, that was not possible either because of my or his work, but there was a chief of the police station and how frequently he communicated with him and conveyed what was said, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P91 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is a mistake. Oh, I'm sorry, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you told us yesterday - that's why I put it to you - that you were privately friends. Transcript page 1128, line 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And after that correction by Mr. Pantelic, that was wrong. You can find that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we move now, please, to 65 ter 732, very quickly, because this is one you mentioned yesterday, or the day before. And I think it's the last few lines in the B/C/S under item 3 that you wanted to draw attention to. And if we can -- in the English, it's on the second page of the translation. No. Yes, second page of the translation, please. Second page. Third page, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Here you ordered the SJB to return a rifle to Nail Hotilovic as he needs it to protect the enterprise. I think this is what you were mentioning yesterday, that this was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what enterprise was he going to protect?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He and his family had a private business which dealt in poultry production, and for many years this small business was in operation. It was in operation during the way [as interpreted] and still is and is rather successful. So the entire -- this entire farm or enterprise was successful during the war, and they enjoyed the protection of the army. And during the operation of disarming, he was -- his weapon was taken away, and then we insisted that they be offered assistance. We insisted both with the military and the police, and as you can see, this, too, came about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He was providing food, in fact, was he? Poultry farm, you said.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had a poultry farm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And those provisions were being used for whom?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the market, whoever used and needed food stuffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it wasn't that these were being given to the army or the police, the poultry?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in part there was probably that too, and I know that they were even donors and that all their food was used. But that this was under any kind of authority that this is how it had to be done, no, that's not how it happened. They were more involved in purchasing poultry from other farmers and they -- because they had a slaughter-house, they would process this meat, so they really worked together with other farmers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to skip the next document because it's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that be marked as an exhibit, that was 732.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P92, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, could we move, please, to the 28th of July, which is 65 ter 736.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Under item 2: "The chief of the SJB has reported that the confiscation of money of individuals who are moving out, it was established that it was being done without anyone's order in an unauthorised manner, and this can have a negative effect on the operation and the reputation of all of us. It was decided that the money confiscated in this manner will be used to help the families of the soldiers killed and other essential costs of the municipality." Who had been unauthorisely [sic] confiscating the money of the individuals that were moving out?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were instances and there was mention of these incidents with -- by people who actually monitored this kind of situation. So there were instances where without their knowledge money was taken away from individuals, and this is what the chief Tepic was actually briefing on, and he asked that something be done about this, primarily because there were such instances of money confiscation and this was being abused --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I'm going to stop you --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in some cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to know -- the question I asked was, who?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to Ljuboje Gavric, I don't know exactly who it was who actually carried this out and who prepared lists of these people and prepared their moving out. I can't recall all the names right now. At this time it was Ljubo Gavric who was in charge of this team.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who, who was stealing the money of people who were moving out? Who was doing it, not who was monitoring the moving out.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot mention a single name with any certainty. Savo would probably have more information on that because he was the one who briefed on it. We did not really go in detail into how that was done, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The moving out, the convoys and the like, who was in charge of security there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security of the convoy was provided by the police station. However, sometimes they were escorted also by some members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. So we've got the police and sometimes the Crisis staff. Of those two groups, who was stealing money --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the members of the Crisis Staff. And I'm sure that neither the police nor the others did that. There is no proof of that. I'm talking now about the people who were preparing lists and making records of the people who are moving out, and I don't know that there were any thefts from these people. And in the convoy itself, I don't know that there were any instances where money was stolen from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's just look at the rest of it. The money that is being confiscated is to be used to help the families of soldiers killed and the other essential costs of the municipality. Do you agree that what we are talking about, according to Savo Tepic, is that money has been stolen. Why wasn't it going to be kept or returned to those from whom it was being stolen?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we didn't know who it was stolen from. Secondly, we didn't know when we would see those people. And in the municipality in order to organise normal every-day life -- because there were shortages of everything, food, electric power, fuel. So every penny was there more than useful because it could be used to buy food and to ensure that people could survive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So anyhow, at this stage the Crisis Staff is accepting that it is unlawfully -- or somebody is unlawfully removing money from those who are moving out?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what we concluded there, that there were instances of unlawful removing of money.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well let's have a look at the meeting of the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that please be made an exhibit, and can we go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P93, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Under item 1: "The problem of the police working unprofessionally in cases of theft and robbery committed by members of the police, who are imposing themselves as a force and authority in their own right, were debated." Which members of the police? The police directly under the command of Savo Tepic, or the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state with full responsibility that when talking about this, these were members of the regular police, or rather, the reserve contingent of the police who were attached to the police station, but these were not members of the Special Police. In this particular instance, that's what it refers to. But as I've said before, there were also earlier instances of members of the Special Police who did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, if that was a problem, and this you can say with full responsibility, as you put it, were not the Special Police, did you say to Savo Tepic, You are in charge of the police station, you must keep these men under control?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both I and the Crisis Staff had very sharp discussions with Savo. He was a special man. He would not allow anyone to interfere in his job and in his work, whereas he was -- he would readily remark other people's work and their jobs. But as far as what was happening at the police station itself, that was something that he was responsible for, and it wasn't our responsibility. And of course, we did call on him to control and have or provide -- ensure control over that police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say it wasn't your responsibility, Mr. Djekanovic, but your responsibility was to ensure, wasn't it, through the police, the safety of the population in Kotor Varos, and if it was being reported that the police were behaving unlawfully, shouldn't you have taken the matter further?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for each problem that we were aware of, we tried to seek a solution immediately. How successful we were under the circumstances, I don't know. If we hadn't reacted as often as we did, the chaos would set in. But we did our best under the circumstances, and we reacted to any such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's go please to, "The Following Conclusions Were Adopted." Item 2: "Commanders of the Special Police unit and other police formations should be asked to provide lists of vehicles allowed freedom of movement. Why did the Special Police have any say in who was allowed freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, this was not decided by the Special Police. Yesterday I said that there were car thefts, that the majority of people were mobilised for various police and army units. And of course in any war zone there is no absolute freedom of movement, so there wasn't one there either. I said that cars were stolen from abandoned houses, driven to Banja Luka, but as for any special permit for movement through check-points these were not issued bit Special Police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the commanders of the Special Police unit should be asked to provide lists of vehicles allowed freedom of movement, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is misinterpretation and misquotation of the document and the witness's statement. I think that in the English translation it says that member of the Special Police and members of other formations are supposed to provide lists of their own vehicles, both official and personal in order for them to be given permits to move around.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read the document in the B/C/S as it is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I object to this, Your Honour. It is not for counsel to give evidence in this case. If he says he thinks there's an error in the translation, he can ask the witness to repeat it and hear what the interpreters say. He is not entitled to give evidence of what is in the document, nor what it actually says. It's a matter for interpreters and the witness. This is about the fourth or fifth time this has happened, and I say I object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I understand your objection and your concern, but the appreciation that the Chamber has for the intervention of Mr. Krgovic was a -- one of the accuracy of the translation of the document and the interpretation, which I anticipate is a not unusual and will be a recurring issue in these proceedings for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have no objection at all if counsel says in his view there's been an error in the translation and he would like it -- but what Mr. Krgovic is doing is actually - additionally, helping the witness - but actually giving the -- what he says is the correct translation. If he says there is an error, then it is open to him to suggest it and not give evidence of what he says that is error is and what it should actually be saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I suggest we cut it off here and turn to the witness. If he would be good enough to read out the part that is contested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 2, to request commanders of the Special Police units and other police formations to provide lists of vehicles that shall be allowed to move.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. That is why I object to this sort of intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So can you tell me why - I'll ask the question again - you were requesting -- or, I'm sorry, the conclusion of the meeting that day was that the commanders of the Special Police unit provide a list of the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for the people who were manning check-points know which vehicles are legitimate, which vehicles are suspicious, or are being used not for the appropriate purposes of army and police. And I mentioned before, there had been car thefts and those cars had been driven to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the Special Police still have authority in Kotor Varos; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which particular authority you are referring to, but the Special Police had combat tasks issued by competent authorities, but they didn't have any special powers. Apart from combat tasks, they didn't have any other particular tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to leave that topic. Item 5: "That all buses available in the municipality should be mobilised for resettling people." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And item 7: "That persons moving away should be informed that they are allowed to take with them not more than 300 Deutschmarks."

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wasn't that confiscation of property belonging to people moving away?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a certain way it could have constituted a certain restriction, but under the circumstances, if a person had a substantial amount of money on themselves, that would have created problems for themselves as well. There were experiences from people who were moving from other territories into our territories, so there was a reverse process in place. Therefore, I cannot provide any justification or a clearly -- reason why this should be like that. There were some objections while people were allowed to take that amount of money with them; however, except for certain individuals, the majority of the people didn't even have that money.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying, sir, that if they had more than that it caused problems, that you were restricting what they could take out for their own benefit?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you understood it correctly. I know that the majority of people never had that much money, so there was no problem in that respect. If this decision was applied at all, I don't think there were any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What you told me literally a minute ago was, "if a person had a substantial amount of money on themselves, that would have created problems for themselves as well." And my question was: By that answer are you intending to say that restricting the amount of money was for their own benefit?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my intention to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then what did you mean by that answer? What problems would it have created for them if they had more money than 300 Deutschemarks?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that this limit on 300 Deutschemarks was a problem for anyone. It was imposed artificially, the people who had more money would have been targeted by robbers and other people who looted houses and took people's property away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's exactly what I thought you were trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Can that be made exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, can I just ask you while we wait for the exhibit number, if anyone was asked to hand over to the Special Police the excess of 300 Deutschemarks which they had on them as they were moving out of Kotor Varos, what happened -- what would happen to that money? You said it would be confiscated, but for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This had never been handed over to the Special Police, and it was not reported to the Special Police either. There were a group of officials led for a time Ljubo Gajic [as interpreted] who registered these things and who paid for the transportation. But I don't know of any instance that anyone turned over an excess of money. If anyone had excess money, they would have left it with a friend, a friend or a relative. I don't know of any single case in which a person handed over excess money to the Special Police, and I'm talking about the people who were leaving. I don't know that anyone handed over a substantial amount of money and that it was appropriated by us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I would like to ask a question as well, Mr. Witness. You said that the people who had more money would have been targeted by robbers and other people who looted houses and took people's property away, but, if I remember exactly, you said somewhat earlier that this was never done by members of the police; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Special Police members never collected the money, nor was it their task to do that. I categorically claim that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. Did they engage in robbing and looting, stealing property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were such cases. Not only by the Special Police, but, yes, initially they were a precursor to this practice, but there were individual cases, members of the Special Police took away primarily moveable property without any authorisations, but there were all kinds of goings-on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just understand that for a minute --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, the exhibit is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P94, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's all right. Thank you very much. All right, can we move, please, to the 15th of August, which is -- yes, this is a -- not on our 65 ter list, so it will be marked for identification, 10109. I just want to ask about one incident there. The last sentence, please, of item 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like -- so there's no argument about the translation, could you read us out what it says in the original B/C/S, Serbian language. Last sentence.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Concerning a group of civilians who were taken from the Vrbanjci sector, it has been ordered for them to be driven to Vlasic, and then directed towards Travnik."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. "A group of civilians taken from..." Now, you were there, does that mean taken -- not a voluntary fleeing if you like, but people actually taken out of, taken from?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you said I was there, I don't know which particular location you referred to. And, two, I attended the session of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was what you were being told and what you then gave instructions to do was that people had been taken from the area, not left voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to reiterate once again. I almost don't know of a single case in which people were forcibly taken out of their homes and taken away. This relates to the problem -- related to the problem in Vecici. On several occasions groups of people were taken to Kotor Varos, and they were asked to be moved to Travnik. Now, what I can say with full responsibility, there was no forcible hoarding of people or forcible transfer of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It doesn't say, does it, a group of people who have voluntarily left or have been fleeing this particular area? It says "taken." Now are you saying that means that no force was involved?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that this group was taken from Vrbanjci to Kotor Varos. You can interpret it in any way you like. Being brought to a place doesn't mean that force was being used.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Instructions were given that they be transported to Vlasic and sent towards Travnik. So did you give those instructions?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the group itself requested that to be done, and thank God we met their request because the majority of people wanted to go to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P95 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then could we have, please, exhibit 65 ter number -- sorry, lost my -- 20th of August. 1883. Item 2. Second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The question of whether persons in custody should also be permitted to leave was addressed, and it was concluded that a list of all such persons should be submitted to the responsible office of the SJB which would decide." Two questions. It was the police who decided who would be released; is that what this says?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you can construe it in that way. Possibly. There were people whose families were leaving, and these people were in custody. And I think that the requests for their release could have been decided by the police station or those responsible for judiciary. So between these two jurisdictions, those who issued orders on detention were actually the ones who could decide on their release.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it your view that people should only be kept in custody if there is a reason to believe they have committed a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the procedure of putting people in custody, I don't know anything about that. This is not my province. Whether they were accused or suspected of having done something, they were put in custody, but as I say, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that please be made an exhibit, and then could we move to the 21st of August, which is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P96, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, as you phrase your next question, we are coming up on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As you formulate your next question, remember we are coming up on a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Item 2, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Apparently this is you speaking, "... matters and problems to be solved to the effect that the pressure and provocation by certain members of the Special Forces unit directed against Muslim and Croat families in order to compel them to leave should be stopped." So a month and a half after Slobodan Dubocanin told that you the Special Forces would be pulled out, they are still operating in Kotor Varos; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And clearly you knew exactly what they were doing, didn't you, because you are the one saying they were carrying out actions to force Muslims and Croats to leave?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were pressures on a number of families who were well off. There were certain special relations between them. Some of them had paid money very early on to certain individuals for them to be escorted to safety. Some remained for a longer period of time and I had no information about any individual cases. All the information that either the War Presidency or my office received, we tried to intervene. There were information sometimes that we received from members from other ethnic communities complaining that they had been maltreated by this or that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's a convenient point. We rise for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, can I ask the last document be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P97, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask again while he is being brought in that we have on the screen 65 ter number 2872.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And while he is being brought in, Ms. Korner, the Chamber reminds counsel, and you in particular, as to the yesterday's exercise in which it was canvassed whether a formal application would have been made by the Prosecution to have the witness who is at present on the stand declared hostile with all of the implications that would flow from that, and as circumstances -- as things turned out, such a formal application did not appear to be necessary. But it appears to the Chamber from the line of questions this morning, and indeed from the last half of yesterday that without such a formal application having been made and ruled upon by the Chamber, that the Prosecution -- well, specifically, you, Ms. Korner, may have slid into the position that you could have been in or would have been in had such an exercise been pursued. And the Chamber's reluctance to intervene in your line of questions, which appeared to us to be leading and, indeed, argumentative in terms of your own witness was because there was no formal objection except for the two or three interventions by Mr. Krgovic on the point. But we think it necessary to emphasise for the record that no application has been made in this respect, and therefore, the Prosecution should be reminded to adhere to the principles as to how questions are led in terms of the witness called by itself. Is the witness on the way in?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think he is just loitering outside, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, he may take the stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us and we've seen from the documents that the Special Police were in Kotor Varos for something in the region of at least two and a half months. So I'd like you to have a look at a photograph, please, which you've been shown before, and could you identify for us, please, first of all Slobodan Dubocanin?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think we better ask him to draw on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you want it zoomed in on so the faces are a bit clearer, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where this photograph was taken. I saw it for the first time on Tuesday when I arrived. The people in the photograph are rather small, so it is nearly impossible for me to recognise anyone with any degree of certainty. The same applies to Slobodan Dubocanin whom I cannot register on the photograph, although I knew him well. Perhaps we could zoom in if there's sufficient quality, otherwise I'm unable to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You gave us an identification on Tuesday, so I'd like you to do the same again, please. We'll zoom in.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Tuesday I said I think it could be this person, although I'm still uncertain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you please mark which one you say is Slobodan Dubocanin. Call him 1, please. Mark 1 by the man you say you think.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I do may be a mistake, an error on my part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sure the Chamber will take that into account. Just mark which one you think is Slobodan Dubocanin.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Djekanovic, could you mark, please. Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My fault. Now, could you mark, please, who Ljuban Ecim is, who you think Ljuban Ecim is, number 2.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible it is this person, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, please, Zdravko Samardzija.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is the one that is the most difficult to recognise him. It is possible that it is this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you mark 3, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have marked him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will need then to become a separate exhibit, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, I appreciate your explanation as to your difficulty in identifying the three individuals that you were asked to mark from the photograph. What I'm not clear about is whether your testimony is that as best you recall they were part of this group that was in the photograph, although you are unable to identify them, or whether you aren't even certain that they would have been part of this group. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand it. First of all, I'm not certain that this entire group as shown here was in Kotor Varos. I have no proof of that. Secondly, I knew all three, Slobodan Dubocanin better than the other two. I know Ljuban somewhat less, and at least I knew Mr. Samardzija. I'm not saying that I could recognise those people now, but this photograph is rather poor. It is Ljubo Ecim for whom I can say with certain certainty that he may be the person in the photograph, I'm not certain about the other two. There isn't sufficient detail in the photograph. If you have another one, I'd be glad to point them out. I know those people, and that is not in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Djekanovic, if I can just have you confirm, what the identity of this group? Who are they? Which unit are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can repeat that I don't know what group this is. This is may have been at one time the Special Police group. I don't know where this photograph was taken. I'm convinced that it was not taken in Kotor Varos. As for who all the members are, I don't know, and I don't know whether this was the exact formation that participated in Kotor Varos and how many of them did. But it is certain that Dubocanin and Samardzija were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm asking about the unit as such. Are these Special Police units, or are they army, or are they -- you know, which units do they appear to be according to their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is the Special Police unit. Although I have to say another thing, there were some red berets as well. I don't know what their establishment was, what their composition was, and whether this includes any red berets which were not in Kotor Varos. I do not question the fact that I do know these three people, but I don't know what the exact formation of this group in Kotor Varos was or compared to this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what I am going to ask you is only because I don't know. You said this could be Special Police unit, do you recognise them on the colour of their berets? Or is that of no importance? How do you -- what does permit you to say that they could be Special Police? Is that the red berets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During a period of time there was a unit called the red berets; I don't know whether they were self-organised. I believe they participated in combat in Croatia. I don't know anything about the formation of this group. I don't know what colour of cap was worn by the Special Police. We were short of almost everything at the time. All units wore different kinds of uniforms, mixed uniforms, but there was a Special Police group in Kotor Varos. Some of them sported different types of caps, hats, uniforms. I cannot tell you with any certainty that indeed this group came in with this precise type of cap.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that be made an exhibit now, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P98, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next could we have up --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document -- maybe not this particular gentleman, but do you recognise the document, Mr. Djekanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I see it I can recognise it and I do not dispute it. There were different kinds of documents as statements, but I don't deny that I'm familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's a document, wasn't it, that had to be signed by people who were leaving the municipality. This gentleman, Mr. Safet Smajlovic, I think that was his father's name. No, first name -- yeah. It was his name, sorry, and his father's name was Ibro. A Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is definitely a Muslim. I don't know him but he is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he says, I declare I'm voluntarily leaving Kotor Varos for the following reasons, I wish to move away and I leave behind my land in Kotor and my destroyed house. And then he declares that he won't join any armed formations. And three copies, one of which sent to the Crisis Staff, one to the population resettlement agency, and one to the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Just on that a last matter --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, we need the English to go further down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was the Autonomous Region of Krajina saying that any records of people leaving had to be sent up to them?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not dispute the authenticity of this document, although I see it for the first time. I know that such documents were produced at the time, but I didn't know whether it was sent to the autonomous region. That is something I cannot say with any certainty. In the different stages of resettlement and in different periods of time, there were different types of registering such people and registering their data. For awhile, that wasn't even done. At a certain stage we wanted to introduce more order and then such statements were being taken. To repeat, I do not dispute that the agency as such forwarded such documents to the Crisis staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I do not question that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P99.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we now move to the -- so sorry, Your Honour, I'm just checking. I think I may have made a mistake. No, I think I've made a mistake, it's not on the list. Yes, sorry it is. 65 ter 10111. Again, it will be marked for identification, Your Honours. Item 4, please, in English, bottom of the first page and over the next.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic requested the War Presidency to give its position on including Muslims and Croats in units of the Army of the Serbian Republic. The War Presidency concluded that as far as this issue is concerned, loyal Muslims and Croats who so request should be assigned on an individual basis." And then: "Savo Tepic said that a similar problem also exists in the police but he believes that it is not yet the right time for including Muslims and Croats in this organ and this should wait for awhile." Now, you told us yesterday that Muslims remained in the police in September from what Mr. Tepic was saying; was that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you understood my words yesterday. My answer did not refer to a certain period of time specifically. I do know, however, that as of the beginning and until his retirement, Rada Tatar remained with the police later on when the reserve police force was being mobilised, because the police force in Kotor Varos prior to the conflict was not numerous. When they started manning the troops, there were certain Muslims who remained with the reserve police force. As for the period prior to this session, I don't know what the situation was, but I'm quite certain that those guys from Galici and the Maslovare Detachment were with the with the police at that time. So to repeat with the police there were certain Muslim forces, members, although not numerous. There was this guy Jasko, he may not have been there from the start, but he was engaged relatively quickly, and he remained with the police throughout the period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right Your Honours, may that be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P100 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, I've just got one last document I want to show you in a minute, but can I just see if we can deal with the background.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The village of Vecici held out, didn't it, for a long time, until the beginning of November?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, late October, early November.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is this right - and Your Honours, I appreciate I'm leading but I don't think there's any dispute about this, and I just want to set the background - there was a series of negotiations with the people who were in Vecici, largely Muslims who were resisting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a strong Muslim unit in Vecici, and the fact that they remained there for so long is significant. Towards the end of October the Serb losses in Vecici alone was over 50, only in that area. It is also correct that there were several negotiations by army representatives. I even participated during one of such events at the bridge by the river from the representatives of Vecici when their surrender and departure were being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, is this right, that at the end of negotiations, and there was an argument about how they were to leave, about 200 men tried to escape and were captured?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly that is partially true. There were far more people in the village, civilians and military, and the negotiations were underway and their final request was that they all be allowed to leave with their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good. But is this right, because I think you've said this before, they were captured and taken to a school in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the -- when there was a breakdown in the communication between the -- within the leadership of Republika Srpska between the commanders and -- of the army -- in the army, they did not allow them to leave with the weapons, and they were not willing on their part to put down their weapons. So one group was transferred -- or actually came to our side and they were taken to -- from Donja Vrbanjci and transported on buses to Travnik as was always the case. How many civilians and how many people remained in Vecici, I don't know, but they were not arrested in Vecici. They set out to break through the lines in several directions from Vecici via Knezevo where strong military forces had there positions towards Travnik, towards Jajce, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I appreciate there is a long history to this, I just want to deal with this one aspect. Were a number of them captured and taken to the school in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a group surrendered and was taken to the school in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you as president of the Crisis Staff informed and did you go to the school on the day that they had been captured?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was actually on site when they were transferred to the school in Grabovica. I was already there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And was it members of the army, not the police, who were dealing with them?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the people there were members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I just want you to look then, this is the final document and final matter I want to ask you about, please, at --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The document number is -- it's the 6th of November of 1992, 65 ter number 10116. Again, it will have to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see under item 2: "President Nedjelko Djekanovic was in Grabovica yesterday monitored the clearing up of the terrain and the cleaning of the school." Was the situation that people had been captured or killed?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the following day, in other words, the evening when these people were brought in there, nothing happened. They were put up in the school and they were searched. I believe some things were taken away from them, maybe some watches or whatever, I don't really know. And they remained that night at the school building. On the next day, the women and children were put on buses and taken to Kotor Varos, and from there on to Travnik. A number of able-bodied men remained in the school building. I don't know exactly how many of them. In the course of that day, there were several killings, but I can't really tell you exactly what the number was, and they weren't killed on the premises of the school itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Djekanovic, what this reads is that you went to monitor the cleaning of the school. What did you find when you got to the school?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was on the third or -- on the second or third day following that. You see, when a number of people, I don't exactly know what the number was, maybe 200 to 300 people, women and children, and as they tried to break through the woods, of course they were not in normal condition when they arrived, and of course there were -- there was damage to the school building. There were many or some families who had lost their loved ones at Vecici. There was also a number of people or a number of families who received the bodies, the charred bodies of their loved ones a few days later from Vecici. So you can imagine what the general situation was like and what the atmosphere was like. And I tried to keep things under control to prevent people from taking -- from avenging their loved ones. And in the end the school year was supposed to begin, and it was normal that we had to put this school in order and prepare it for the new school year. And as was the custom, I tried to actually visit and inspect all the schools and make sure that they could start with their school year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you find any blood in the school when you went there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- there were some traces of blood, but there wasn't a lot of blood. Maybe some people were beaten in all this commotion. There was some blood on the walls; but that there was major beating up in the schools going on, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's all I ask. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, what would ordinarily happen at this stage is that the lawyers for the accused persons be invited to cross-examine you if they wish, but for reasons -- for certain administrative reasons we have to interpose a witness at this stage in the course of these proceedings. And it is regretted that the inconvenience to you would be that you -- you are not released now as a witness, although you are stood down until possibly Monday or even possibly until later next week. So at this stage you are being excused from the courtroom but not released, and I would repeat the admonitions that I would have given to you on yesterday's adjournment and the adjournment of the day previous, that because you are not yet released, you cannot communicate with the lawyers on either side at all, and in terms of any conversations or discussions you may have with persons other than the lawyers, it cannot relate to your testimony -- to the testimony that you are giving. Do you understand what I've just said? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand fully what you've just said, but this is a problem for me because I have business to attend to and I have a family. But in any case, I have come as summoned by the Court and I will comply with this order as well, but I would also appeal to you to, if at all possible, try and complete my questioning today. Of course if not, I can't do anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
